project_inclusion.range_basis: Native to East Asia, introduced in Texas; NON_NATIVE/INVASIVE learner comparison; exclude entirely from Texas-native metrics.

look_here_first: FOLLOW ONE FLOWER STALK BACK TO ITS NODE. In Japanese honeysuckle, flowers are paired, two at a time, arising from LEAF AXILS along the shoot rather than a terminal whorl. The strongly two-lipped flowers start pale white and may age yellow. The mature berries turn dark/black (the others red).

morphology_keys.habit: Evergreen to semievergreen twining vine with opposite distinct elliptic to ovate short-petiolate leaves and usually hairy young stems; common escaped/invasive Texas vine.
morphology_keys.leaf_arrangement: Opposite simple leaves with entire to near-entire margins; petiole lengths and fused terminal bracts vary by species.
morphology_keys.flower: Paired axillary flowers with long strongly two-lipped white fading-yellow corollas ~45–57 mm and projecting reproductive parts; not terminal condensed whorls.
morphology_keys.fruit: Dark nearly black mature berries commonly ~6–8 mm, supporting Japanese honeysuckle compared with the two red-fruited native species.
diagnostic_sequence: Follow the flower stalk to determine AXILLARY paired flowers versus TERMINAL whorls.
Check one lateral flower: short two-lipped (~17–20 mm) / long tubular (~38–48 mm) / long strongly two-lipped (~45–57 mm).
Examine whether fused terminal bracts occur; do NOT use fused bracts alone for native pair.
If berries are ripe, note red-or-orange vs black—but berries are supporting evidence.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Versus both natives, AXILLARY pairs rather than TERMINAL condensed whorls. White-yellow aging and fragrance support but do not prove ID. Dark ripe berries rather than red; small hairs on young petioles/stems. Keep explicit introduced label.
